meta.title: Physical-quantity glossary
meta.note: Meaning, this project's value, the typical range and why it is chosen, and how that range differs for telecom / satellite / quantum work versus other fields.

symbols.name: Optical wavelength
symbols.meaning: The carrier light's wavelength; sets diffraction, atmospheric scattering, and detector response.
symbols.range: Free-space optics: ~800 nm, ~1064 nm, or 1550 nm. This project fixes 1550 nm.
symbols.why: 1550 nm is eye-safe at higher power, sits in the atmosphere's low-loss window, scatters less off aerosols than visible light (Kruse/Kim exponent), and reuses mature, cheap telecom lasers/detectors/fibre.
symbols.domain: Telecom/satellite FSO almost always pick 1550 nm for those reasons. General optics/astronomy span UV→IR freely; lidar often uses 532/1064 nm. Quantum labs sometimes prefer shorter wavelengths where single-photon detectors are most efficient — a tension this direct-detection design sidesteps.

symbols.name: Beam divergence half-angle
symbols.meaning: How fast the transmitted laser beam spreads; smaller means a tighter, farther-reaching beam.
symbols.why: 10 μrad keeps geometric spreading loss manageable at 550 km, but a tighter beam demands finer pointing (PAT), so it trades against pointing budget.
symbols.domain: Satellite laser-comm lives in the microradian regime because links are thousands of km. RF antennas think in degrees (milliradians+); a laser pointer is ~1 mrad — 100× wider than this.

symbols.name: Beam waist
symbols.meaning: The beam's narrowest radius, at the transmitter: w₀ = λ/(2θ_C).
symbols.why: Fixed by λ and θ_C; a smaller divergence gives a larger waist and slower far-field spreading.
symbols.domain: A derived quantity specific to Gaussian-beam optics; RF engineering has no direct analogue.

symbols.name: Beam radius at the receiver
symbols.meaning: The spot radius after propagating the slant range L; grows ~linearly with distance.
symbols.why: Because w_L (metres) ≫ aperture a_R (5 cm), only ~(a_R/w_L)² of the power is collected — the origin of the >30 dB geometric loss.
symbols.domain: This metre-scale spot over a centimetre aperture is why FSO link budgets are dominated by geometry, unlike fibre (no spreading) or RF (much wider beams but larger antennas).

symbols.name: Receiver aperture radius
symbols.meaning: Radius of the ground telescope collecting the beam.
symbols.range: Satellite FSO ground optics: a few cm (CubeSat-class, e.g. TBIRD ~0.2 m) up to ~1 m (Micius ground station).
symbols.why: A small aperture is cheap/light and lets you deploy many stations, but collects a smaller fraction of the already-weak key signal — an unresolved SWaP trade-off here.
symbols.domain: Astronomy uses metre-to-10-metre apertures for faint light; this project deliberately picks the small, cheap end to argue a multi-station network.

symbols.name: Geometric spreading loss
symbols.meaning: Fraction of transmitted power reaching the aperture, from beam spreading: h_g = [erf(ν_R)]².
symbols.range: Tens of dB (very lossy) for LEO FSO.
symbols.why: It scales ~1/L², so lower passes (longer range) are much worse; it is the single largest term in the link budget.
symbols.domain: Uniquely severe in free-space optics; fibre has none, and RF free-space path loss, while large, is offset by high antenna gains.

symbols.name: Atmospheric transmission
symbols.meaning: Beer-Lambert transmission through the air: h_l = exp(−σ_total·L_atm).
symbols.value: ≈ −9 dB (clear, zenith) to ≈ −18 dB (clear, 30°); ~−100 dB in heavy rain.
symbols.why: Set by visibility and rain rate along the slant path; low elevation lengthens the path (1/cos ζ).
symbols.domain: Remote sensing / atmospheric science model exactly this extinction. In this project cloud is treated as a separate binary outage, not folded into h_l.

symbols.name: Clear-air extinction coefficient
symbols.meaning: Per-km attenuation from aerosols/molecules (Kruse/Kim): σ = (3.912/V)(λ/550)^(−q).
symbols.why: Inversely tied to meteorological visibility V; the wavelength factor makes 1550 nm scatter less than visible.
symbols.domain: A staple of atmospheric optics / lidar; identical machinery to remote-sensing atmospheric correction.

symbols.name: Rain extinction coefficient
symbols.meaning: Per-km attenuation from raindrops: β = αR^ρ (dB/km), σ_rain = β/4.343.
symbols.why: The sub-linear exponent (ρ < 1) reflects Mie scattering by large drops; calibrated on real tropical measurements, not textbook constants.
symbols.domain: Tropical FSO needs region-specific coefficients; temperate ITU rain models differ. RF rain fade (Ka-band) uses a related but distinct power law.

symbols.name: Rain rate
symbols.meaning: Instantaneous rainfall intensity during raining hours.
symbols.value: Converted from monthly totals: R = R_month/(30·24·f_rain).
symbols.range: Light drizzle ~0.1 mm/h to tropical downpour 30–50+ mm/h.
symbols.why: Tropical rain is intermittent, so monthly totals must be concentrated into the hours it actually rains (f_rain).
symbols.domain: Meteorology/hydrology quantity; FSO and Ka-band RF both care because both suffer rain fade, unlike lower RF bands.

symbols.name: Meteorological visibility
symbols.meaning: Horizontal distance at which contrast drops to a threshold; a proxy for aerosol load.
symbols.value: Derived here as V = 15 − 10·P_cloud (no historical visibility record exists).
symbols.why: It directly sets σ_clear; a derived estimate is used because ERA5 has no visibility variable.
symbols.domain: A standard weather-station output; here it is inferred, a stated modelling limitation.

symbols.name: Satellite altitude
symbols.meaning: Height of the LEO satellite above the ground.
symbols.range: LEO ~300–2000 km; this project fixes 550 km.
symbols.why: The channel model is parameterised for one altitude; mixing shells would need altitude-dependent tables.
symbols.domain: 550 km is the modern mega-constellation sweet spot (low latency, manageable drag). GEO comms sit at 35 786 km; the ISS at ~400 km.

symbols.name: Zenith / elevation angle
symbols.meaning: ζ is measured from straight up; elevation ε = 90° − ζ is measured from the horizon.
symbols.why: Low elevation lengthens both the geometric range and the atmospheric path; a 30° (or safer 40°) mask bounds the loss and QBER.
symbols.domain: Universal to any ground-to-space link (comms, GNSS, radio astronomy). GNSS often accepts 5–15°; QKD wants higher for signal quality.

symbols.name: Ground-coverage radius
symbols.meaning: Radius on the ground within which a station can see the satellite above the mask.
symbols.why: Sets which city pairs (within 2·R_cov) can share one pass — the DUAL/SF split.
symbols.domain: A coverage-geometry staple; the same footprint idea underlies cellular NTN planning.

symbols.name: Rytov variance (scintillation)
symbols.meaning: Strength of turbulence-induced intensity fluctuations along the path.
symbols.why: The slant path to LEO stays weak, so log-normal fading applies; the v3 coefficient is 2.25 (plane-wave slant path).
symbols.domain: Central to astronomy's 'seeing' and adaptive optics, and to FSO. Fibre and RF do not have optical scintillation.

symbols.name: Refractive-index structure parameter
symbols.meaning: Local turbulence strength versus altitude (Hufnagel-Valley profile).
symbols.why: The ground layer decays within ~500 m, so high-altitude wind (not C_n²(0)) dominates the LEO slant-path integral.
symbols.domain: A term shared by astronomy (site seeing) and FSO; its exotic m⁻²ᐟ³ units come from Kolmogorov turbulence theory.

symbols.name: Transmit optical power
symbols.meaning: Average optical power leaving the transmitter.
symbols.why: 1 W is a realistic small-payload figure; higher power eases the link budget but costs SWaP and raises cross-talk (which grows as P²).
symbols.domain: Quantum single-photon QKD works at the femtowatt/photon level; this direct-detection SIKD design instead uses a strong classical-style carrier, which is why power is in watts, not photons.

symbols.name: Key-channel modulation index
symbols.meaning: Depth of the quantum-key subcarrier's modulation.
symbols.why: The source SIKD manuscript's feasible region opens for m_K ≳ 0.1; 0.15 drops QBER below even the 10⁻³ target while leaving budget for data.
symbols.domain: A subcarrier-multiplexing parameter specific to this SIKD architecture; classical SCM systems tune it purely for SNR, here it also trades against the key's security.

symbols.name: Data-channel modulation index
symbols.meaning: Depth of the classical data subcarrier's modulation.
symbols.why: Higher m_D raises data throughput but leaks more cross-talk into the key receiver (σ_CT² ∝ m_D²) — the core SIKD tension.
symbols.domain: In plain SCM you would push m_D high for capacity; here it is capped because it directly attacks the quantum channel's QBER.

symbols.name: Filter isolation
symbols.meaning: How well the RF/optical filter separates the key and data subcarriers.
symbols.why: Finite isolation lets the data channel leak in as cross-talk; better isolation directly lowers QBER (σ_CT² ∝ 10^(−Iso/10)).
symbols.domain: A filter-engineering figure; its impact here is amplified because the leaked signal lands on a security-critical quantum channel.

symbols.name: Raw bit rate
symbols.meaning: Symbol/bit rate of the link; sets the noise bandwidth Δf = R_b/2.
symbols.range: Satellite FSO downlinks: Mbps to hundreds of Gbps (TBIRD hit 200 Gbps).
symbols.why: It scales the absolute secret key rate (SKR_bps = SKR_norm·R_b) and the receiver noise bandwidth.
symbols.domain: Comms-wide quantity; FSO reaches far higher rates than RF thanks to optical bandwidth.

symbols.name: Receiver noise (std. dev.)
symbols.meaning: Total electrical noise: shot + thermal + background + cross-talk.
symbols.value: Sum of four variances; cross-talk dominates when the link is strong.
symbols.range: Set by detector, temperature, bandwidth, and link strength.
symbols.why: It sets the decision thresholds and hence QBER; the v3 cross-talk fix (/8) cut the dominant term four-fold.
symbols.domain: Every receiver has shot+thermal noise; the cross-talk term is special to this shared-detector SIKD design and, unusually, grows with signal power (∝ P²).

symbols.name: Cross-talk noise variance
symbols.meaning: Data-channel power leaking into the key receiver: ∝ (R_e P_T m_D h_g h_l)²·10^(−Iso/10)/8.
symbols.value: Ranges from ~0.5× to ~290× thermal noise across elevation.
symbols.why: Because it scales as P², it dominates exactly when the link is strongest (high elevation) — a counter-intuitive, defining SIKD result.
symbols.domain: Ordinary noise falls or is flat with signal; this term rising with signal is the signature quirk of multiplexing data and key on one detector.

symbols.name: Quantum bit error rate
symbols.meaning: Fraction of sifted key bits where Bob disagrees with Alice; the master security indicator.
symbols.range: Must stay below 11% (BB84) to distil any secret key; stricter protocols want ≤ 10⁻³.
symbols.why: Eavesdropping and noise both raise QBER; below threshold a positive secret key survives after error correction and privacy amplification.
symbols.domain: A QKD-specific metric with a hard security threshold — unlike a classical BER, where 10⁻³ is merely 'poor', here 11% is a wall.

symbols.name: Secret key rate
symbols.meaning: Rate of provably-secret key bits: SKR_norm = P_sift[1 − 2H₂(QBER) − χ_E].
symbols.range: Zero at QBER ≈ 11%; up to tens of Mbps here.
symbols.why: The mutual information minus error-correction leakage minus Eve's information; it collapses steeply near the QBER threshold.
symbols.domain: The headline output of any QKD system. Real satellite QKD (Micius) delivered kbps; this direct-detection design models Mbps because it uses a strong carrier, not single photons.

symbols.name: Sift probability
symbols.meaning: Probability a received sample is confidently decoded (falls outside the dual-threshold guard zone).
symbols.value: Averaged over turbulence by 20-point Gauss-Hermite quadrature.
symbols.range: 0 to 0.5 (half the samples are the key basis).
symbols.why: A wider guard zone lowers errors but sifts out more samples — a yield-vs-error trade set by the threshold scale ζ_scale = 2.
symbols.domain: Sifting is intrinsic to QKD (basis reconciliation / thresholding); no classical-comms analogue.

symbols.name: Eve's Holevo information
symbols.meaning: The maximum information an eavesdropper can hold about the key.
symbols.range: 0 (no attack) up to values that zero the SKR.
symbols.why: It is what privacy amplification must remove; setting it to 0 characterises performance, not adversarial security.
symbols.domain: A quantum-information quantity (Holevo bound); has no classical counterpart.

symbols.name: Binary entropy function
symbols.meaning: H₂(p) = −p·log₂p − (1−p)·log₂(1−p); the information cost of a bit-flip probability p.
symbols.why: It appears twice in the SKR bound (mutual information and error-correction leakage), which is why SKR hits zero at QBER ≈ 11%.
symbols.domain: A Shannon-information staple used across coding theory; here it directly sets the QKD security threshold.

symbols.name: Cloud probability & availability
symbols.meaning: P_cloud is the fraction of hours with thick cloud (link off); availability A = 1 − P_cloud.
symbols.value: A ranges 10.7% (Kuala Lumpur, Nov) to 96.5% (Bangkok, Feb).
symbols.range: Wildly location/season dependent in the tropics.
symbols.why: Thick cloud blocks the optical beam entirely, so availability is governed by cloud, not rain; A is invariant to the rain fraction.
symbols.domain: Optical links treat cloud as total blockage; RF satcom passes through cloud almost unaffected — the fundamental reason tropical optical QKD is hard.

symbols.name: Handover / acquisition cost
symbols.meaning: Time lost re-acquiring a satellite when a station switches links.
symbols.why: Every re-assignment loses delivered key; charging it fairly is why weather-aware scheduling shows a small net cost.
symbols.domain: FSO needs seconds to re-acquire a narrow beam; RF beam-steering is far faster, so this penalty is an optical-link-specific concern.
